after: ## What Question 2 asks you to do
alt: Question 2 asks how strong the evidence is, in three jobs: reliability, whether it can be trusted; support, whether it backs the claim it is used for; and gaps, what other evidence would confirm or overturn the claim. Most weak answers stop at reliability. Worth 15 of 45 marks, about 30 minutes.
caption: Trustworthy evidence can still give weak support; test the link and the gaps too.

alt: A two-column margin note pairs each piece of evidence with the claim it supports: a survey percentage with “most people want this policy”, a named doctor’s quotation with “the policy improves health”, and one family’s story with “costs fall hardest on the poor”. Mapping first avoids treating opinions as evidence and missing buried evidence.
caption: List every piece of evidence beside the claim it is meant to support.

after: ## Step 2: test each piece by its type
alt: Six evidence types with the questions that expose strengths and weaknesses: statistics, surveys or polls, expert testimony, personal accounts, case studies and research studies. Strengths count as evaluation as well as weaknesses.
caption: Different kinds of evidence fail in different ways, so change the questions you ask.

after: ## Step 3: test the link between evidence and claim
alt: Evidence can be accurate yet give weak support because the step to the claim is unsafe. Five gaps: scope, from one place or group to everyone; measure, from something nearby to something else; cause, from correlation to causation; selection, only examples that fit; and strength, from a small effect to “proves”.
caption: This step separates the top band: check the bridge, not just the evidence.

alt: A useful suggestion states what evidence (children’s dental or hospital records before and after the tax, compared with a similar country), why it is needed (to test whether lower sales changed health), and what result would strengthen or weaken the claim.
caption: Say what evidence, why, and what result would change the verdict.

alt: A 15-mark plan: an opening judgement of the main claim and your verdict, two or three evidence paragraphs each with a strength, a weakness and the link to the claim, a gaps paragraph on specific missing evidence, and a weighed concluding verdict.
caption: Open and close with a verdict; go deep on the evidence that matters most.

alt: A fictional column claims a sugar tax is working. Its evidence gives some support to the claim that sugary drink sales fell, weak support to the claim that health improved because sales measure purchases not health, and very weak support to the recommendation that other countries copy it.
caption: The same evidence can support a narrow claim and fail a broad one.
